newsitem.title: USA: Corporations sing a country song.
newsitem.headline: Corporations sing a country song.

text.p: Corporate America is hanging its hat on country music this year as never before, even as the sound that made Nashville famous has faded a bit among music lovers.
Leading the pack of company executives reaching out for the country dollar is former investment banker William Farley, Chairman and CEO of Fruit of the Loom Inc.

His "All Star CountryFest" last year in Atlanta was the biggest outdoor concert ever -- surpassing even the original Woodstock. This year, his company is sponsoring a year-long 60-date tour of country stars highlighted with another CountryFest June 14 at Texas International Raceway in Dallas-Fort Worth.
Retail country music sales slipped last year by 12 percent from 1995, dropping to $67 million from $76 million.
But Tim Wipperman, executive vice president and general manager of Warner/Chappell Music publishers, says the dip is only a "flattening."
"We were growing so rapidly it had to slow down. I don't think it's anything but a market correction. And corporate sponsorship is an advertising mechanism that's working," he added.

"Corporations have done their demographics. There is a different type of country fan from years ago and they're going after the business and getting it," said Wipperman, who discovered superstar Alan Jackson two years ago.
Advertising is no stranger to country music.
In the 1940s Prince Albert Tobacco sponsored the radio network portion of the Grand Ole Opry show beamed out to rural families huddled around radios tuned in to station WSM in Nashville.
The curtain that rang down between acts on weekends was emblazoned "Martha White Flour" and just before World War II Opry stars toured on a "Camel Caravan" sponsored by R.J. Reynolds Co.

Farley says his 1996 promotion paid off, with Fruit of the Loom scoring 20 percent to 40 percent higher in brand awareness and purchase intent among likely country fans in tour markets compared with the general population.

CBS-TV and The Nashville Network will broadcast special CountryFest programming again this year. Three national radio syndicates -- Westwood One, Ron Huntsman Entertainment and Backstage Productions -- will produce special programmes on the tour and a multi-media website on the Internet will feature video and music clips of headliners and concert updates.

Elsewhere in the corporate sponsorship ranks, Mobil has become the first major oil company to explore country music commercially. Top award winners Brooks & Dunn have teamed up with Reba McEntire for a blockbuster tour kicked off in Memphis and moving on to 85 cities nationwide.

"We at Mobil want to talk to our customers in a language they understand best," says George Madden, manager of lube business at Mobil, "and that's country music, a language that talks to their hearts and souls."

Martha White Foods is sponsoring this year's tour by bluegrass award winner Alison Krauss and Union Station. Their buses with the Martha White label are travelling to five cities a week for performances in Wal-Mart Stores Inc. parking lots. A Country Music Television crew is taping the concerts in 260 cities for a one-hour special.

As a side promotion, Wal-Mart customers who buy Krauss's latest album "So Long, So Wrong," also will receive a booklet on the history of bluegrass music and a bonus five-track CD featuring bluegrass favourites.

And Jackson, who has sold more than 23 million albums, has just been named official spokesperson for Ford Motor Co. trucks. Jackson signed an exclusive partnership with Ford to promote the trucks through TV and radio commercials and print ads.
Paul Morel, F-Series Brand Manager for Ford, notes that "country music is especially popular among full-size pickup buyers."

Although not new to country sponsorships, Kraft Foods Inc., is kicking off an 85-city tour headlining Vince Gill to benefit Second Harvest, a national food bank network. Kraft, which has sponsored the annual Country Music Association's Awards Show, will incorporate a cookhouse and cooking demonstrations with the tour.
